persons.name: L W Payne
persons.note: THE 1835 POLL LIST ALONE. Read from poll_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G2a), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll_1835 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1835 and nothing says when they came. THE BOUND FALLS AFTER THE SCENE DATE and the record says so rather than narrowing it: the earliest source that names this person is later than 1 July 1835, so they may have arrived after the day this scene models. present_on_scene_date is `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of 1835 — “Payne, L. W.” (poll_1835_056, line 343). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Payne' agrees with the entry's forenames; 2 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

persons.name: Mrs. H. Sherman
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name ''RS. H. SHERMAN,' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 3 December 1834, column 21. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `dressmaker` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Sherman, Howard | Letter. | December 29, 1852. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0830, printed page 200), admitted 1852-12-29 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Sherman' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins H. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

The return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office on 1 July 1834 was set three times in the Chicago Democrat — 1834-07-02 p3 c2, 1834-07-09 p1 c2 and 1834-07-16 p1 c2 — and two of those settings print 'samuel E. Toby' where the middle one prints 'samuel. Toby' and sets no middle initial at all. THE OWNER RULED ON 2026-09-24 (T-1528) that a present initial may absorb an ABSENT one at the same entry of the same list, bounded exactly as T-0392's unread-initial ruling was, and the gazetteer now keys this person on 'Samuel E. Toby' until then, which is the ABSORBED side: after the merge, nothing this record cites read the name that way, and the surviving reading was sitting in this card's own press_evidence row. THE ID DOES NOT MOVE WITH THE NAME — `toby_samuel` is a handle every crosswalk cites and not a claim (rule N5, T-1139), and the family name it was minted off is the one the card still reads. AND THE FIELD NOW FOLLOWS THE MERGED RECORD (T-1562). `letter_list_returns` is one date PER RETURN and not per printing, so three impressions of the 1 July 1834 return put ONE date in it, and it is the first printing that carries the name: 1834-07-02. Reading the last printing in instead would date the evidence by a compositor's re-run; carrying both ends would say the office held letters for this man in two separate returns, which is the strongest thing a letter list can say about residence and is not what happened.
